name: Celandine Green
lede: Celandine Green is a pale grey-green from Werner's system of colors for naturalists, where it stood at number 46 and was illustrated with a moth, a leaf and a gemstone.

sections.title: Werner's number 46
sections.body:
In Werner's system, as Syme published it, Celandine Green is color 46 among the greens [1][2]. Every color in the system was tied to three examples, one from animals, one from plants and one from minerals [2][3]. For Celandine Green they were the wings of the moth *Phalaena margaritaria* (now *Glyphodes margaritaria*), the back of coltsfoot leaves (*Tussilago farfara*), and beryl [1][3].

The mineral example in Baty's plate is a beryl set within white topaz in an 1898 illustration [3]. The recipe the system gave was verdigris green mixed with ash grey [3]. Its neighbor, Mountain Green, was mostly emerald green, with a good deal of blue and a touch of grey-yellow [3]. See also [[mountain-green]] and [[verdigris-green]].

sections.title: Which celandine?
sections.body: The name points at a plant, but the sources we hold do not say which celandine Werner meant, so we do not guess [3]. What the system does show is where to look: turn over a coltsfoot leaf and its reverse is where Baty shows the color [3].

sections.title: Later charts
sections.body: Other charts kept the name. Ridgway's 1912 atlas has Celandine Green on plate 47, and his version is darker and greener, near #8AA18C [4]. The ISCC-NBS system puts it in block 150, and Maerz and Paul, whom our library follows, date the name to 1807 and place it on plate 29, block B 4 [4]. Our swatch is an approximation of Werner's aged print, not a measurement of the paint he saw [4]. Its nearest named color in the library is Ash, at a distance of 3.4 [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 1,118 (4.7%) hold this swatch within six units of ΔE2000 over at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed [5]. In 94% of them it plays the highlight role, the lightest part of the palette [5]. It is a color of pale grounds and skies more than of subjects, though the archive cannot say what each match depicts.

It peaks in Impressionism, where 26 of 140 paintings match (18.6%, about 4 times the average) [5]. Britain leads the countries with 84 of 593 (14.2%) [5]. Of the six strongest matches, three are beach and coast scenes by Boudin, such as [[painting:nga-61362|Figures on the Beach]], and the best is Ito Jakuchu's *Kanzan and Jittoku*, 74% of the canvas [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test.

openers: Turn over a coltsfoot leaf: its reverse was Werner's plant example of Celandine Green [3].
Celandine Green was mixed, on paper, from verdigris green and ash grey [3].
